$comment: Shared behavioural fixtures for the capability allow-list matcher. Two byte-identical copies exist: code/tests/sg_caps_match/caps-match-fixtures.json, read by the OCaml suite that is the authority for the semantics, and code/src/hermes/caps-match-fixtures.json, read by code/src/hermes/lib/api/capsMatch.test.ts, the TypeScript port used for UI gating. hermes holds a copy rather than a symlink out of its tree because code/src/hermes has to be self-contained -- the image's UI stage copies that directory alone -- and .github/workflows/lint.yml fails if the two drift. Edit both. A semantic change on either side fails CI on both. Add a case here rather than to only one suite.

matches.$comment: The empty list denies everything. It is NOT an all-negation list, so it gains no implicit '*' -- transcribing the all-negation rule first inverts deny-all into grant-all.
An all-negation list carries an implicit leading '*': everything except what it names.
A pattern is a literal prefix with an optional single trailing '*'.
Matching is anchored on both ends, so a prefix glob does not match a value that merely contains it.

A mid-string '*' is refused at the input boundary by is_valid_pattern and can never be stored -- but the matcher itself does not consult parse_glob, so if one were present it would act as a wildcard. Pinned so the OCaml matcher and the TypeScript port agree even on input validation would have rejected.
Regex metacharacters are literal. '.' must not act as a wildcard.
Tenant ids are UUIDs, so escaping '-' is load-bearing rather than theoretical.
A negation wins over a positive that also matches.

grants_all.$comment: Only a bare '*' with no negations grants every value.
An all-negation list materializes '*' but keeps its negations, so it does not grant all.
